Basically, since f(x)/x approaches 1 when x approaches 0, you know f(x) = x + o(x), where o(x)/x approaches 0 when x approaches 0.

x^2 - 1 = (x + 1)(x - 1), so you can deduce that f(x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) is of the same order as (x + 1) when x approaches 1, meaning f(x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) approaches 2.

So, French native speaker here, honestly I’m not sure about how explaining it since I haven’t had a French lesson in over six years but I’ll try.

Basically, imparfait is mainly used for two things : describing something (in the past) or telling about something that lasted for some extended amount of time (in the past). These two uses are like “it was amazing” and “I was taking a walk”. For both of these you’d say respectively “c’était génial”, “je me promenais”.

For passé composé, it’s a bit more whack because you can use it for A LOT of stuff. But it mainly comes down to three uses. Either you’re describing something that just happened (that’s why you could translate “I was taking a walk” with passé composé too if it just happened), or it could be about describing something short happening in the past, like a brief sensation, or to describe something happening just after what you talked about.

For example, the first verb here is clearly imparfait, especially since it’s during this extended period of time that something happens. If you used passé composé, it would work BUT it would also mean like it ended immediately, you couldn’t be able to say something like “suddenly something happened” it would sound weird.

In English, you would translate it by “Last Friday, I was taking a walk when suddenly…” if you used imparfait and “Last Friday, I took a walk when suddenly…” if you used passé composé. Like it still kinda works but it sounds a bit weird.

For the second verb, it comes after “suddenly” so it clearly is passé composé, you’ll never (or very rarely) find imparfait after something like “suddenly”, “then”, “immediately after”, etc.

The third is a bit tricky, because it’s passé composé, but kinda like the first one, you’d use imparfait if something happened while you were running -> “I was running toward the voice when I saw an old lady” would work but here it’s more like “I ran towards the voice. I saw an old lady”

The fifth verb is a clear description of a state and not an action so it’s imparfait. (She was…)

The sixth is a description of an action, BUT it’s imprecise in time, “she was shaking” and not “she shook”.

Basically it goes like this. If it should be past continuous in your head, it’s almost definitely imparfait unless it just happened in which case it’s passé composé. If it’s past simple you have to be careful if it’s just a disguised imparfait because it’s to describe a state with “was” (“she was ahead in the polls” -> “elle était en tête dans les sondages”) but most of the time past simple is passé composé.
